title: NASA’s Hubble Views a Cosmic Skyrocket
caption: Herbig-Haro 110 jet, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: HH 110 · constellation Orion · about 1,300 light-years away (source figure)

recognition.text: NASA Hubble image release (STScI). No published audience rating.

story: A wispy, semi-transparent blue jet of gas stretches from the lower right to the upper left. This is Herbig-Haro 110, a fountain of hot gas, launched by a newborn star, that strikes the dense heart of a molecular hydrogen cloud and bounces off. Its plumes are light-years across, and it lies about 1,300 light-years away in Orion.

Herbig-Haro objects vary in shape, but most share a basic plan. A forming star, surrounded by a disc of dust and gas, fires twin jets of heated gas in opposite directions. Where a jet rams into colder gas, material piles up, heats sharply and glows in a curved front called a bow shock.

HH 110 bends that pattern. Astronomers have repeatedly searched for the star that drives it and found nothing. They now think a neighboring jet, HH 270, grazes a much denser, colder cloud core and is deflected at about a 60-degree angle. It fades from view and then reappears as HH 110.

understand.summary: The image combines data from Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys and Wide Field Camera 3. NASA shows F814W (I) in blue, F658N (hydrogen-alpha) in cyan, F110W (J) in green and F160W (H) in red.
understand.eye: Two of the four filters record infrared light the eye cannot see, and the combined exposures total 2.6 hours.

explore: Inside the jet, fast blobs of gas catch up with slower ones and collide, creating hot blue ridges where new shocks form. By measuring the positions and speeds of these blobs, astronomers can trace them back to when they were launched, which can give insight into how the source star has gathered mass over time.
